Eastward
ēst'wărd
adv. and a. (toward the east; in Scripture the direction of Eden, of the tabernacle door, and of the returning glory)
From east (Anglo-Saxon east, the quarter of the dawn) plus the directional suffix -ward, meaning turned toward. The Hebrew for east, qedem, also means front and ancient — the Hebrew orients himself facing the sunrise, so that east is before him and the past is before him too.

Biblical Definition

Eastward is the most theologically freighted compass point in Scripture. The garden is planted there: “the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Gen 2:8) — and when the man is driven out, cherubim are set at the east of the garden to keep the way of the tree of life, so that the road back to God lies east and is barred. The tabernacle repeats the geography deliberately: the only door faces east, and immediately before it “shall be Moses, and Aaron and his sons, keeping the charge of the sanctuary” (Num 3:38) — the priesthood camped exactly where the cherubim stood, guarding the same approach. And Ezekiel sees the return: “the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” (Eze 43:4) — the glory that had departed eastward comes back by the same road. To Abram, standing between promise and possession, the LORD says, “Lift up now thine eyes… northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward” (Gen 13:14), and the whole land is given by looking.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines eastward as toward the east, in the direction of the rising sun — and notes the east as the quarter of the sunrise, whence the ancient orientation of temples and of maps.

expand to see more

EASTWARD, adv. Toward the east; in the direction of east; as, to move eastward.

EAST, n. The point in the heavens where the sun is seen to rise at the equinox, or the corresponding point on the earth.

2. In Scripture, the east is often put for the front, as the Hebrews reckoned the quarters facing the rising sun.

Note. Hence in Hebrew the same word denotes the east and that which is before or ancient.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:8 — "And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed."

Num 3:38 — "But those that encamp before the tabernacle toward the east, even before the tabernacle of the congregation eastward, shall be Moses, and Aaron and his sons, keeping the charge of the sanctuary for the charge of the children of Israel; and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death."

Eze 43:4 — "And the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east."

Gen 13:14 — "And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:"

Modern Corruption

The sacred orientation of Scripture is either dismissed as borrowed Ancient Near Eastern architecture or seized upon by mystics as a spiritual technique.

expand to see more

The historical-critical habit is to note that other ancient temples also faced east and conclude that Israel simply absorbed regional convention. The direction of the argument is wrong. Scripture gives its own reason for the eastward door, and it is a narrative reason: the way back into the presence of God was closed at the east of Eden, and every subsequent sanctuary reopens that same approach under guard, under blood, and by appointment. The tabernacle is not borrowed architecture; it is a theological argument in fabric and gold, and Moses is told to make it after the pattern shewed him in the mount (Exo 25:40).

The opposite error treats compass directions as channels of spiritual power — praying eastward for enlightenment, arranging a room for spiritual flow. That is not devotion but divination, and the same Ezekiel who saw the glory return by the east gate had earlier seen men in the temple “with their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east” (Eze 8:16), which is named as an abomination. The eastward door means what God says it means: there is one way in, He appointed it, and He has posted a guard at it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English east + -ward; rendering Hebrew qedem (H6924), east, front, aforetime, and mizrach (H4217), the place of the sun's rising.

expand to see more

Hebrew qedem (H6924) — east, front, ancient time; the Hebrew faces the sunrise, so before him is both east and the past.

Hebrew miqqedem — “eastward” in Gen 2:8, and “at the east” of the garden where the cherubim are placed (Gen 3:24).

Hebrew mizrach (H4217) — the rising, the east quarter; from zarach, to rise, said of the sun.

Anglo-Saxon -weard — turned toward; the suffix of eastward, homeward, toward.

Mat 2:1 — the wise men come “from the east”, and Mat 24:27 makes the lightning that cometh out of the east the figure of Christ's coming.

Usage

"“A garden eastward in Eden” — and the way back barred at the east by cherubim."

"“Before the tabernacle… eastward” — the priests camped where the cherubim stood."

"“By the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” — the glory returning by the road it left."
